But once they start to please you, even briefly, they take over. They corrupt your mind and pull you off the right path. So choose what is best without hesitation and stick to it. People say the most profitable thing is best. If they mean profitable to you as a rational being, then hold to that. But if they just mean profitable to you as an animal, reject it. Guard this principle carefully. Don't let the attractive appearance of external things fool you. This way you can see things clearly.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain
thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man,
to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that
requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before
all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of
virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never
sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is
chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for
life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus
compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even
now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action,
which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long,
this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such
intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Never consider something profitable if it forces you to break your word, lose your dignity, hate anyone, become suspicious, curse, lie, or crave things you must hide behind walls or curtains. But the person who puts his rational mind and spirit first — and the sacred truths of virtue that flow from it — will never complain or cry out, never sigh. He will never lack for solitude or company. Most important of all, he will live without desire or fear. Whether he enjoys life in his body for a long time or short, he doesn't care. If he had to die right now, he would be as ready for that as for any other decent action. His whole life long, he has one concern: that his mind stays focused on thoughts and goals fitting for a rational, social being.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst
not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered:
nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no
malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of
such an one, death can never surprise as imperfect; as of an actor, that
should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, a man
might speak.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: In a mind that is truly disciplined and clean, you won't find anything foul or impure, or anything festering. Nothing servile or fake. No partial loyalties. No bitter hatred. Nothing harmful. Nothing hidden. Death can never catch such a person unprepared. It's not like an actor dying before the play is finished.

meditations_book-03.originalText: Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a rational creature. The end and object of a rational constitution is, to do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected towards men, and in all things willingly to submit unto the gods. Casting therefore all other things aside, keep thyself to these few, and remember withal that no man properly can be said to live more than that which is now present, which is but a moment of time.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Treat your ability to form opinions with respect, because everything depends on it. Don't let your opinions create thoughts that go against nature or what it means to be a thinking person. The purpose of being rational is simple: don't act rashly, be kind to people, and accept what the gods give you. Put aside everything else and focus on these few things. Remember that no one really lives longer than this present moment, which lasts only an instant.

meditations_book-03.originalText: Whatsoever is besides either is already past, or uncertain. The time therefore that any man doth live, is but a little, and the place where he liveth, is but a very little corner of the earth, and the greatest fame that can remain of a man after his death, even that is but little, and that too, such as it is whilst it is, is by the succession of silly mortal men preserved, who likewise shall shortly die, and even whiles they live know not what in very deed they themselves are: and much less can know one, who long before is dead and gone.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Everything else is either already past or uncertain. The time any person lives is short. The place where he lives is just a tiny corner of the earth. Even the greatest fame a person can have after death is small. And that fame, whatever it is, gets passed down by foolish mortal people who will soon die themselves. Even while they're alive, they don't know what they really are. How could they possibly know someone who died long ago?

meditations_book-03.originalText:
To these ever-present helps and mementoes, let one more be added,
ever to make a particular description and delineation as it were of
every object that presents itself to thy mind, that thou mayest wholly
and throughly contemplate it, in its own proper nature, bare and naked;
wholly, and severally; divided into its several parts and quarters: and
then by thyself in thy mind, to call both it, and those things of which
it doth consist, and in which it shall be resolved, by their own proper
true names, and appellations. For there is nothing so effectual to beget
true magnanimity, as to be able truly and methodically to examine and
consider all things that happen in this life, and so to penetrate
into their natures, that at the same time, this also may concur in our
apprehensions: what is the true use of it? and what is the true nature
of this universe, to which it is useful? how much in regard of the
universe may it be esteemed? how much in regard of man, a citizen of the
supreme city, of which all other cities in the world are as it were but
houses and families?
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Add one more practice to these daily reminders. When anything comes to your mind, describe it clearly and completely. Look at it as it really is — bare and simple. Break it down into its parts. Then name both the thing itself and what it's made of by their true names. Nothing builds real courage like being able to examine everything that happens in life this way. Look deep into the nature of things. At the same time, ask yourself: what is this really for? What role does it play in the universe? How important is it compared to everything else? How important is it for a human being — a citizen of the greatest city, which makes all other cities look like small houses?

meditations_book-03.originalText:
What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth
it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper
virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth,
faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest? Of everything
therefore thou must use thyself to say, This immediately comes from God,
this by that fatal connection, and concatenation of things, or (which
almost comes to one) by some coincidental casualty. And as for this, it
proceeds from my neighbour, my kinsman, my fellow: through his ignorance
indeed, because he knows not what is truly natural unto him: but I know
it, and therefore carry myself towards him according to the natural law
of fellowship; that is kindly, and justly. As for those things that of
themselves are altogether indifferent, as in my best judgment I conceive
everything to deserve more or less, so I carry myself towards it.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: What am I focused on right now? What is it made of? How long will it last? Which virtue should I use here? Should I be gentle, brave, honest, faithful, sincere, content, or something else? Get used to saying this about everything: This comes straight from God. This happens because everything is connected. Or this is just chance. And this other thing comes from my neighbor, my family member, my fellow human. They act from ignorance because they don't know what's natural for them. But I do know. So I treat them according to the natural law of human fellowship — with kindness and justice. As for things that don't matter either way, I deal with them based on how much I think they're worth.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of
right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix
any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit
unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope
or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak,
contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and
from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Focus on what is happening right now. Follow what is right and reasonable with care, strength, and gentleness. Don't get distracted by other things. Work only to keep your spirit clean and pure. Hold onto this without hoping or fearing anything. In everything you do or say, be content with simple truth. If you do this, you will live happily. And no one can stop you from living this way.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready
at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a
readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and
whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou
must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between
these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto
God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other
side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Just as doctors keep their tools ready for emergencies, keep your principles ready to understand both divine and human things. Whatever you do, even the smallest tasks, remember the connection between the sacred and the everyday. You can't succeed in worldly matters without thinking of God. And you can't handle divine things without considering human affairs.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral
commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those
excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid
up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and
giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for
thyself, as thou oughtest to do.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Don't fool yourself. You will never live to read your moral commentaries, or the histories of famous Romans and Greeks, or those excerpts from books you've been collecting for your old age. So hurry up and finish what matters. Give up these empty hopes and help yourself now, while you still can.

meditations_book-03.originalText:
To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done
(which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what
these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not
understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses
naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the
soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: To steal, to plant, to buy, to rest, to see what needs doing — this kind of seeing doesn't use the eyes, but a different kind of sight. People don't understand what these words really mean or how many ways they can be taken. The body, the soul, the mind. Just as the senses belong naturally to the body, and desires and feelings belong to the soul, so do beliefs and principles belong to the mind.

meditations_book-03.originalText: To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero were. To follow reason for ordinary duties and actions is common to them also, who believe not that there be any gods, and for their advantage would make no conscience to betray their own country; and who when once the doors be shut upon them, dare do anything.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish: Both humans and animals can have fantasies and imaginings. To be violently pulled around by lusts and desires is what wild beasts do — and monsters like Phalaris and Nero. Even following reason for everyday duties is common to people who don't believe in gods, who would betray their country for personal gain, and who will do anything once no one is watching.

meditations_book-03.originalText: If therefore all things else be common to these likewise, it follows, that for a man to like and embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him, and not to trouble and molest that spirit which is seated in the temple of his own breast, with a multitude of vain fancies and imaginations, but to keep him propitious and to obey him as a god, never either speaking anything contrary to truth, or doing anything contrary to justice, is the only true property of a good man. And such a one, though no man should believe that he liveth as he doth, either sincerely and conscionably, or cheerful and contentedly; yet is he neither with any man at all angry for it, nor diverted by it from the way that leadeth to the end of his life, through which a man must pass pure, ever ready to depart, and willing of himself without any compulsion to fit and accommodate himself to his proper lot and portion.
meditations_book-03.plainEnglish:
If all other things are shared by everyone, then a good person should accept everything that happens to them without complaint. They should not trouble the spirit in their heart with useless thoughts and fantasies. Instead, they should keep that spirit calm and obey it like a god. They should never speak lies or act unjustly.

This is what makes someone truly good. Even if no one believes they live honestly, conscientiously, or happily, they should not get angry about it. They should not let it pull them away from the path that leads to the end of life. A person must walk this path with purity, always ready to leave, and willingly accepting their fate without being forced to.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural
temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and
affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may
be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at
first it intended. For it never doth absolutely addict and apply itself
to any one object, but whatsoever it is that it doth now intend and
prosecute, it doth prosecute it with exception and reservation; so that
whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even
that afterwards it makes its proper object. Even as the fire when it
prevails upon those things that are in his way; by which things indeed a
little fire would have been quenched, but a great fire doth soon turn to
its own nature, and so consume whatsoever comes in his way: yea by those
very things it is made greater and greater.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: The ruling part of your mind, when it's in its natural state, handles all worldly events in a special way. It can easily shift and adapt to what's possible and within its power when it can't get what it first wanted. It never locks itself completely onto any one goal. Whatever it's working toward, it holds with some flexibility. So when things turn out differently than planned, it makes those new circumstances its target instead. It's like fire when it encounters obstacles. A small fire would be put out by them, but a great fire turns everything to its own nature and consumes whatever gets in its way. In fact, those very obstacles make it burn even stronger.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according
to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Don't do anything rashly or at random. Do everything according to the most exact and perfect rules of your craft.

meditations_book-04.originalText: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: People look for private places to escape — country villages, the seashore, mountains. You yourself often crave such places. But you should know this comes from the simplest kind of thinking. Whenever you want, you can retreat into yourself and find rest, free from all troubles. No one can retreat to a better place than his own soul. This is especially true if he has already prepared good things within himself. When he looks inward, he can immediately find perfect peace and calm. By calm I mean a proper, orderly way of being that is free from confusion and chaos. Give yourself this retreat constantly, and refresh yourself.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto. For what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend? and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto ashes? It is time for thee to make an end.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Keep these ideas simple and basic. When you remember them, they should be enough to clear your mind and send you back to your work content with whatever you face. What are you upset about? Are you angry at people's bad behavior? Remember that all rational beings were made to help each other. It's part of justice to put up with them. They don't mean to do wrong. And think about how many people who once held grudges, suspected others, hated, and fought bitterly are now long dead and turned to ash. It's time to let it go.

meditations_book-04.originalText: As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou dost consider that thy mind and understanding, when once it hath recollected itself, and knows its own power, hath in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently, or whether harshly and rudely), no interest at all, but is altogether indifferent: and whatsoever else thou hast heard and assented unto concerning either pain or pleasure?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: When bad things happen to you in life, why be upset? Remember our basic choice: either the universe has purpose, or it's just random atoms bumping around. Either way, we proved that the whole world is like one city. As for your body, what is there to fear? Your mind, once it gets itself together and knows its own strength, doesn't care whether life goes smoothly or roughly. It stays detached. Remember what you learned about pain and pleasure — they don't really matter.

meditations_book-04.originalText: But the care of thine honour and reputation will perchance distract thee? How can that be, if thou dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of men are they, that will commend thee?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: But maybe you worry that caring about your honor and reputation will distract you? How can that be, if you look back and think about how quickly everything gets forgotten? Think about the vast stretch of eternity that came before and will come after. Think about how empty praise really is. Think about how people change their minds and judge things differently. Think about how small the place is where your reputation matters. The whole earth is just one tiny point. The part where people live is an even smaller part of that. And in this small part, how many people are there who will actually praise you? What kind of people are they?

meditations_book-04.originalText: What remains then, but that thou often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this little part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from distraction, and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider all things, as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to withdraw thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand. One, that the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but stand without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next, that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many changes and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an eyewitness of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: What's left then? Keep practicing this withdrawal into the small, true part of yourself. Above all, don't let yourself get scattered. Don't chase anything too desperately. Stay free and look at everything clearly — as someone who cares about virtue, as someone naturally kind and social, as a citizen, as someone who will die. Among the key ideas to remember when you pull back from the world, keep these two close at hand. First: things themselves can't touch your soul. They stay outside, quiet and still. All the noise and trouble comes only from your opinions about them. Second: everything you see right now will change very soon and disappear. Remember how many shifts and changes you've already witnessed in your lifetime. This world is nothing but change. This life is nothing but opinion.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then
is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If
reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is
to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law,
then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one
commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other
commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this
common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto
us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from
some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is
imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that
likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth
not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced
unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence
my understanding hath proceeded.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: If all humans can understand and reason, then the ability to reason is shared by everyone. If reason is universal, then the reasoning that tells us what to do and what not to do is also universal. If that's true, then we share the same law. If we share the same law, then we are fellow citizens. If we are fellow citizens, then we belong to the same community. If that's so, then the world is like one great city. What other community could include all people as members? From this shared city we get our understanding, our reason, and our law. Where else could they come from? Just as the earthly part of me comes from common earth, and the wet part comes from water, and my breath and life have their source, and the dry and fiery parts in me have their origin — nothing comes from nowhere, and nothing disappears into nothing — so my understanding also comes from some shared source.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a
mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing
surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal
events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto,
not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper
constitution of man himself.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Birth is a mystery of nature's wisdom, and so is death. We are made from mixed elements, and we return to those same elements again. No one should be ashamed of this. It is part of the series of events that happen to thinking creatures like us. It is not wrong or out of place. It fits with how we are naturally made.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity
proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that
would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum,
remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall
both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names
and memories shall be remaining.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Certain things must happen for certain reasons. That's just how it works. Someone who doesn't want these things to happen is like someone who wants a fig tree to grow without any sap or water. Remember this: very soon, both you and he will be dead. And not long after that, even your names and memories will be gone.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such
thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot
make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly
or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and
therefore necessary.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Take away opinion, and no one will think they've been wronged. If no one thinks they've been wronged, then there is no such thing as being wronged. What doesn't make a person worse can't make their life worse. It can't hurt them inside or outside. Nature made it this way because it had to be so.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if
thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it. I say not only in right
order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice
and as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth
of everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as thou hast begun,
and whatsoever thou dost, do it not without this proviso, that it be a
thing of that nature that a good man (as the word good is properly
taken) may do it. This observe carefully in every action.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever happens in the world happens justly. If you pay close attention, you will see this. I don't just mean things follow in logical order. I mean they happen according to justice — like fair distribution based on what everything truly deserves. Keep noticing this as you have started to do. Whatever you do, make sure it is something a good person would do. Watch for this in every action.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth,
or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see
what it is in very truth.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Don't accept the story that someone who wrongs you wants you to believe. Look at what actually happened and see it for what it really is.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do
nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme
part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee. And
secondly, if any man that is present shall be able to rectify thee or to
turn thee from some erroneous persuasion, that thou be always ready to
change thy mind, and this change to proceed, not from any respect of any
pleasure or credit thereon depending, but always from some probable
apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be
furthered; or from some other such inducement.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Keep these two rules always ready. First, do nothing unless your rational mind — the ruling part of you — suggests it for the good of other people. Second, if someone can correct you or show you where you're wrong, be ready to change your mind. But don't change for pleasure or to look good. Change only when you see good reason — when it serves justice or helps everyone, or for some other worthy cause.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if
thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Do you have reason? I do. Then why don't you use it? If your reason does its job, what more could you need?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now
shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot
thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational
substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated.
Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops
first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Until now you have existed as a separate part. Soon you will dissolve back into the common substance of the one who first created you. Or rather, you will return to that original rational substance from which all things come and spread out. Many small pieces of incense are placed on the same altar. One burns up first, then another. In the end it all comes to the same thing.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of
them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring
of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an
ape.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: In ten days, if it happens, you will be thought of as a god by the same people who now, if you return to your principles and honor reason, will think of you as nothing more than a brute or an ape.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs
over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Not as though you have thousands of years to live. Death hangs over you. While you are still alive, while you can, be good.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know
what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only
what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in
Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others,
but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant
agitation.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: How much time and peace you gain when you don't worry about what your neighbor said or did or tried to do. Instead, you focus only on your own actions — making sure they are just and good. As Agathos said: Don't look around at other people's faults, but run straight ahead without getting distracted or worked up.

meditations_book-04.originalText: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct. But suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory with them should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to thee after thou art dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise? But only for a secret and politic consideration, which we call οἰκονομίαν, or dispensation.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Someone who craves fame and praise after death doesn't think this through. The people who remember him will soon die too. And the people who come after them will also die. Eventually all memory of him will disappear completely — passed along by people who admired him briefly before they died, until the chain finally breaks. But even if the people who remember you could live forever, and your memory with them — what would that matter to you? I won't even ask what good it does you when you're dead. What good does praise do you even while you're alive? It only serves some hidden political purpose.

meditations_book-04.originalText: For as for that, that it is the gift of nature, whatsoever is commended in thee, what might be objected from thence, let that now that we are upon another consideration be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatsoever it be, and in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and goodly, it is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either better or worse. This I understand even of those things, that are commonly called fair and good, as those which are commended either for the matter itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or truth; or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those, either becomes good or fair, because commended; or dispraised suffers any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile if it be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a tree?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever good qualities you have by nature — forget about praise for now. We're thinking about something else. Anything that is truly beautiful or good is beautiful and good in itself. It doesn't need praise to complete it. So when something gets praised, that doesn't make it better or worse. I mean this even for things we normally call beautiful — things praised for their material or craftsmanship. As for what is truly good, what more does it need beyond justice or truth? What more than kindness and humility? Do any of these become good or beautiful because someone praises them? Do they get damaged when criticized? Does an emerald become worse if no one compliments it? What about gold, ivory, or purple cloth? Is there anything — even something as ordinary as a knife, a flower, or a tree — that changes because of what people say?

meditations_book-04.originalText: If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How is the earth (say I) ever from that time able to Contain the bodies of them that are buried? For as here the change and resolution of dead bodies into another kind of subsistence (whatsoever it be;) makes place for other dead bodies: so the souls after death transferred into the air, after they have conversed there a while, are either by way of transmutation, or transfusion, or conflagration, received again into that original rational substance, from which all others do proceed: and so give way to those souls, who before coupled and associated unto bodies, now begin to subsist single.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Some people don't believe souls survive death. They ask: how could the air hold all these souls forever? But I ask back: how does the earth keep holding all the buried bodies forever? Here's how it works. Dead bodies change and break down into something else. This makes room for new dead bodies. The same thing happens with souls. After death, souls move into the air. After spending some time there, they change or dissolve or burn up. They get absorbed back into the original rational substance that all souls come from. This makes room for new souls that are just separating from their bodies.

meditations_book-04.originalText: This, upon a supposition that the souls after death do for a while subsist single, may be answered. And here, (besides the number of bodies, so buried and contained by the earth), we may further consider the number of several beasts, eaten by us men, and by other creatures. For notwithstanding that such a multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it were buried in the bodies of the eaters, yet is the same place and body able to contain them, by reason of their conversion, partly into blood, partly into air and fire. What in these things is the speculation of truth? to divide things into that which is passive and material; and that which is active and formal.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: This answers the question, assuming souls exist separately for a time after death. Think about this: besides all the human bodies buried in the earth, consider how many animals we and other creatures eat every day. Despite this huge number being consumed and buried inside the bodies that eat them, the same space can hold them all. This happens because they change form — some becoming blood, some becoming air and fire. What is the real truth here? Divide everything into two parts: what is passive and material, and what is active and gives form.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire,
to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the
true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Don't get sidetracked. With every impulse and desire, do what is right. And always be careful to see every thought that comes up for what it really is.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me;
nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto
thee is seasonable. Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be
esteemed as happy fruit, and increase. O Nature! from thee are all
things, in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend. Could he say
of Athens, Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the
world, Thou lovely city of God?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever is right for you, O World, is right for me. Nothing can be wrong or badly timed for me if it's the right time for you. Whatever your seasons bring, I will always see as good fruit and growth. O Nature! All things come from you, all things exist in you, and all things return to you. If someone could say of Athens, 'You lovely city of Cecrops,' shouldn't you say of the world, 'You lovely city of God?'

meditations_book-04.originalText:
They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt
live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man
to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as
reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command
and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the
goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually
proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either
speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs
follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble,
and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition
suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the
number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off
actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary
for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and
cut off.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish:
People often say: Don't meddle with too many things if you want to live happily. Nothing is better than sticking to necessary actions only. Do only what reason commands — the kind of reason that belongs to a creature born to live in society. This brings two kinds of cheerfulness: the kind that comes from doing good, and the kind that comes from doing fewer things.

Most of what we say and do is unnecessary. Cut these things out and you'll have more free time and less trouble. So before every action, ask yourself: Could this thing I'm about to do be unnecessary? Don't just cut out unnecessary actions. Cut out unnecessary thoughts too. That way you'll prevent the unnecessary actions that would have followed.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee. Thou hast had experience of that other kind of life: make now trial of this also. Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto perfect simplicity.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Try living like a good person. Someone who accepts whatever happens to come his way in this world. Someone who feels satisfied with doing the right thing now and having good intentions for the future. See how that way of life sits with you. You've tried the other way of living. Now test this one. Stop making trouble for yourself. Make your life simple.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Doth any man offend? It is against himself that he doth offend: why should it trouble thee? Hath anything happened unto thee? It is well, whatsoever it be, it is that which of all the common chances of the world from the very beginning in the series of all other things that have, or shall happen, was destinated and appointed unto thee. To comprehend all in a few words, our life is short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion and justice. Use recreation with sobriety.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Does someone offend you? They are only hurting themselves. Why should that trouble you? Has something happened to you? It is well. Whatever it is, it was meant for you from the very beginning. It was part of the pattern of all things that have happened or will happen. To say it simply: life is short. We must make the most of the present moment with wisdom and fairness. Enjoy yourself, but stay balanced.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all
disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though
confused, yet still it is a comely piece. For is it possible that in
thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world
there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? and all things in it
too, by natural different properties one from another differenced and
distinguished; and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy,
one to another united, as they are?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Either this world is a beautiful, ordered whole — everything arranged and governed by certain laws — or it's a mixture that seems confused but is still beautiful. How could there be any beauty in you while the whole world is nothing but disorder and confusion? All things in it are different from each other by their natural properties, yet they're connected throughout and united by natural sympathy.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an
hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish
disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a
fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world,
that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well,
that wonders at the things that are done in it?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Some people are bitter or mean. Others are weak. Some are hard and cruel. Others are savage and inhuman. Some follow like sheep. Others act like children. Some are dull, dishonest, vulgar, deceitful, or tyrannical. So what? If someone is a stranger to the world who doesn't understand how it works, why not also be a stranger who is amazed by what happens in it?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are
sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding.
He poor, that stands in need of another, and hath not in himself all
things needful for this life. He an aposteme of the world, who by being
discontented with those things that happen unto him in the world,
doth as it were apostatise, and separate himself from common nature's
rational administration. For the same nature it is that brings this
unto thee, whatsoever it be, that first brought thee into the world. He
raises sedition in the city, who by irrational actions withdraws his own
soul from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: A true runaway is someone who flees from reason — the thing that makes us social beings. A blind person is someone who cannot see with their mind's eye. A poor person is someone who needs others and doesn't have within themselves what they need for life. A disease in the world is someone who gets upset with what happens to them. By being discontent, they separate themselves from nature's rational order. The same nature that brings you whatever happens now is the same nature that brought you into the world. Someone who stirs up trouble in the city is someone whose irrational actions pull their soul away from the one common soul we all share as thinking beings.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without
so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked,
neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith
one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and
yet I depart not from reason.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: One person has no coat. Another has no books. Yet both still practice philosophy. "I am half naked and have no bread," says one, "but I don't abandon reason." But I say: "I lack good teaching and instruction, yet I don't abandon reason either."

meditations_book-04.originalText:
What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to
affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life
as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs
unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either
tyrannically or servilely towards any.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever skill or work you have learned, try to love it and find comfort in it. Live the rest of your life as someone who trusts the gods completely with himself and everything he owns. As for other people, don't be either a tyrant or a slave to anyone.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Consider in my mind, for example's sake, the times of Vespasian:
thou shalt see but the same things: some marrying, some bringing up
children, some sick, some dying, some fighting, some feasting, some
merchandising, some tilling, some flattering, some boasting, some
suspecting, some undermining, some wishing to die, some fretting and
murmuring at their present estate, some wooing, some hoarding, some
seeking after magistracies, and some after kingdoms. And is not that
their age quite over, and ended? Again, consider now the times of
Trajan. There likewise thou seest the very self-same things, and that
age also is now over and ended. In the like manner consider other
periods, both of times and of whole nations, and see how many men, after
they had with all their might and main intended and prosecuted some one
worldly thing or other did soon after drop away, and were resolved into
the elements. But especially thou must call to mind them, whom thou
thyself in thy lifetime hast known much distracted about vain things,
and in the meantime neglecting to do that, and closely and unseparably
(as fully satisfied with it) to adhere unto it, which their own proper
constitution did require. And here thou must remember, that thy carriage
in every business must be according to the worth and due proportion of
it, for so shalt thou not easily be tired out and vexed, if thou shalt
not dwell upon small matters longer than is fitting.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Think about the times of Emperor Vespasian, for example. You'll see the same things: people getting married, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting, celebrating, doing business, farming, flattering others, bragging, being suspicious, scheming, wishing they were dead, complaining about their lives, courting lovers, hoarding wealth, seeking office, seeking power. And now that whole era is over and done with. Think about the times of Trajan. You see exactly the same things there too. That age is also over and ended. Look at other periods the same way — whole eras and nations. See how many people threw themselves completely into some worldly pursuit, only to die soon after and return to dust. But especially remember the people you knew in your own lifetime who got worked up over pointless things. Meanwhile they ignored what they should have been doing — the work their own nature required of them. Remember this: how much energy you put into something should match how much it actually matters. That way you won't get exhausted and frustrated by spending too much time on small things.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus; not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Adrianus, then Antoninus Pius: all these in a short time will be out of date, and, as things of another world as it were, become fabulous. And this I say of them, who once shined as the wonders of their ages, for as for the rest, no sooner are they expired, than with them all their fame and memory. And what is it then that shall always be remembered? all is vanity.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Words that were once common are now strange and forgotten. The same thing happens to the names of famous men. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus — then later Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Hadrian, then Antoninus Pius. Soon all these names will be forgotten too. They will seem like myths from another world. And these were the brightest stars of their time. As for everyone else, they die and their fame dies with them right away. So what will be remembered forever? Nothing. It's all meaningless.

meditations_book-04.originalText: What is it that we must bestow our care and diligence upon? even upon this only: that our minds and wills be just; that our actions be charitable; that our speech be never deceitful, or that our understanding be not subject to error; that our inclination be always set to embrace whatsoever shall happen unto us, as necessary, as usual, as ordinary, as flowing from such a beginning, and such a fountain, from which both thou thyself and all things are. Willingly therefore, and wholly surrender up thyself unto that fatal concatenation, yielding up thyself unto the fates, to be disposed of at their pleasure.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: What deserves our care and effort? Only this: that our thoughts and choices be fair; that our actions be kind; that our words be honest; that our understanding be clear; that we always accept whatever happens to us as necessary, normal, and natural — flowing from the same source that made us and everything else. So give yourself over completely to this chain of fate. Surrender to the way things unfold.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence;
all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves,
incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change
and alteration. Use thyself therefore often to meditate upon this, that
the nature of the universe delights in nothing more, than in altering
those things that are, and in making others like unto them. So that we
may say, that whatsoever is, is but as it were the seed of that which
shall be. For if thou think that that only is seed, which either the
earth or the womb receiveth, thou art very simple.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Everything that exists now, day by day, changes constantly. All the things we remember, and our minds and memories themselves, are always shifting. Think about this often: everything that exists comes from change. The universe loves nothing more than changing what is and making new things from the old. So whatever exists now is just the seed of what will come next. If you think seeds only come from the earth or the womb, you're missing the point.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to
that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and
perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external
accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou
shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is,
to be just in all his actions.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: You are ready to die, but you still haven't reached that perfect simplicity. You are still troubled by many things. You still feel fear and worry about what might happen to you. You are not yet as kind to everyone as you should be. You are not yet like someone whose only focus and wisdom is to be just in everything they do.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and
those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are
afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Look at people and see what state their minds are in. Even those the world calls wise — see what they run from in fear, and what they chase after.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist,
nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy
body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul. Wherein
then, but in that part of thee, wherein the conceit, and apprehension
of any misery can subsist? Let not that part therefore admit any such
conceit, and then all is well. Though thy body which is so near it
should either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction,
yet let that part to which it belongs to judge of these, be still at
rest; that is, let her judge this, that whatsoever it is, that equally
may happen to a wicked man, and to a good man, is neither good nor evil.
For that which happens equally to him that lives according to nature,
and to him that doth not, is neither according to nature, nor against
it; and by consequent, neither good nor bad.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Your troubles can't exist in another person's mind. They can't exist in your body either — your body is just the house where your soul lives. So where can your troubles exist? Only in the part of you that forms ideas about suffering. Don't let that part create such ideas, and you'll be fine. Even if your body gets cut or burned or starts to rot, keep the part that judges these things calm. Let it remember this: whatever happens equally to both good people and bad people is neither good nor evil. Anything that happens the same way to those who live naturally and those who don't is neither natural nor unnatural. So it's neither good nor bad.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living
substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are
terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion
as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that
are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of
connection and concatenation all things happen.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Think of the world as one living being with one soul. All things flow into one shared awareness. They move together as if guided by one mind making decisions. Everything that exists helps cause everything else to exist. See how all things are connected and linked together.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as
Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up
and down?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: What are you, apart from that better and divine part, but as Epictetus said, a miserable soul stuck carrying a dead body around?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to
attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and
swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in
the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away,
another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Being changed cannot hurt you. And getting created through change is not really a benefit either. The age and time of the world is like a flood or fast river, made up of all the things that happen. As soon as something appears and passes away, another thing takes its place. And that too will soon be out of sight.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature,
as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of
the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and
whatsoever else ordinarily doth unto fools use to be occasion either
of joy or sorrow. That, whatsoever it is, that comes after, doth always
very naturally, and as it were familiarly, follow upon that which was
before. For thou must consider the things of the world, not as a loose
independent number, consisting merely of necessary events; but as a
discreet connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There
is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession,
but an admirable correspondence and affinity.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Whatever happens in the world is as natural and ordinary as roses in spring or fruit in summer. Sickness and death are the same way. So are gossip and betrayal and whatever else makes fools happy or sad. Whatever comes next always follows naturally from what came before. You have to see the things of this world not as random events that just happen to be necessary. See them as a careful connection of things arranged in order and harmony. In the world's events, there is not just one thing after another. There is a beautiful pattern and kinship.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let that of Heraclitus never be out of thy mind, that the death
of earth, is water, and the death of water, is air; and the death of
air, is fire; and so on the contrary. Remember him also who was
ignorant whither the way did lead, and how that reason being the thing
by which all things in the world are administered, and which men are
continually and most inwardly conversant with: yet is the thing, which
ordinarily they are most in opposition with, and how those things which
daily happen among them, cease not daily to be strange unto them, and
that we should not either speak, or do anything as men in their sleep,
by opinion and bare imagination: for then we think we speak and do, and
that we must not be as children, who follow their father's example; for
best reason alleging their bare καθότι παρειλήφαμεν; or, as by
successive tradition from our forefathers we have received it.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Keep Heraclitus in mind: earth dies and becomes water, water dies and becomes air, air dies and becomes fire, and so on backwards. Remember also the man who didn't know where the path led. Think how reason rules everything in the world. Men live with reason constantly and intimately. Yet they fight against it most of all. Daily events never stop seeming strange to them. We should not speak or act like sleepwalkers, driven by mere opinion and fantasy. When we do that, we only think we're speaking and acting. And we must not be like children who copy their father simply because "that's how we learned it" or "that's what our ancestors passed down."

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt
certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert
extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather
to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the
difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die
rather many years after, than the very next day.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Imagine if a god told you: 'You will die tomorrow, or the next day.' Unless you were completely cowardly, you wouldn't think it was some great benefit to die the day after tomorrow instead of tomorrow. What's the difference, really? For the same reason, don't think it matters much whether you die many years from now or the very next day.

meditations_book-04.originalText: Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves. How many astrologers, after that in great ostentation they had foretold the death of some others, how many philosophers after so many elaborate tracts and volumes concerning either mortality or immortality; how many brave captains and commanders, after the death and slaughter of so many; how many kings and tyrants, after they had with such horror and insolency abused their power upon men's lives, as though themselves had been immortal; how many, that I may so speak, whole cities both men and towns: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others innumerable are dead and gone. Run them over also, whom thou thyself, one after another, hast known in thy time to drop away. Such and such a one took care of such and such a one's burial, and soon after was buried himself. So one, so another: and all things in a short time.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Keep this thought always in mind: how many doctors who once looked so serious and frowned dramatically over their patients are now dead themselves. How many fortune-tellers who made a great show of predicting other people's deaths. How many philosophers after writing so many elaborate books about death and immortality. How many brave generals after killing so many others. How many kings and tyrants who abused their power over people's lives as if they would live forever. How many entire cities — Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others — are gone completely. Think also of the people you have known personally, one after another, who have died in your lifetime. This person arranged that person's funeral, and soon after was buried himself. One after another. Everything passes quickly.

meditations_book-04.originalText: For herein lieth all indeed, ever to look upon all worldly things, as things for their continuance, that are but for a day: and for their worth, most vile, and contemptible, as for example, What is man? That which but the other day when he was conceived was vile snivel; and within few days shall be either an embalmed carcass, or mere ashes. Thus must thou according to truth and nature, throughly consider how man's life is but for a very moment of time, and so depart meek and contented: even as if a ripe olive falling should praise the ground that bare her, and give thanks to the tree that begat her.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Here's what matters: always see worldly things for what they are. They last only a day and are worth almost nothing. Take man, for example. Just yesterday he was conceived from something disgusting. In a few days he'll be either an embalmed corpse or ashes. You must think about this honestly. Human life lasts only a moment. So leave this world gentle and satisfied, like a ripe olive that falls and thanks the ground that held it and the tree that made it.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though
the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are
those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: You must be like a cliff by the sea. The waves beat against it constantly, but it stands firm. And around it, those crashing waves grow calm and quiet.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I,
to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither
wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come.
For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having
such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why
then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But
however, canst thou, O man! term that unhappiness, which is no mischance
to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature
of man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature? What
then hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which
hath happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or
temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from
anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession
whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto
her,) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow
remember henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is
that hath happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself,
as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great
happiness.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Poor me, this bad thing happened! No, wait — lucky me. This thing happened, and I can handle it without falling apart. I'm not hurt by what's happening now. I'm not afraid of what's coming next. This could have happened to anyone. But not everyone could get through it without breaking down. So why call this bad luck instead of good luck? Can you really call something unlucky if it doesn't harm human nature itself? Can you call it a disaster if it doesn't go against what we're meant to do? What have you learned about what humans are supposed to do? Does this thing that happened stop you from being fair? Or brave? Or self-controlled? Or wise? Or careful? Or honest? Or humble? Or free? Does it stop you from having any of the things that make human nature complete and satisfied? Here's what to remember: whenever you feel sorry for yourself, use this rule. Whatever happened to you is not really a misfortune. But handling it well — that's true happiness.

meditations_book-04.originalText:
It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual
remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the
examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a
long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose
deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last?
as Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their
lifetime having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The
whole space of any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is,
with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society
of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee
altogether as a matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward;
behold, what an infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee;
and as infinite a chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is
so infinite, what difference can there be between that which liveth but
three days, and that which liveth three ages?
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: This is a simple but powerful way to overcome the fear of death. Think about people who lived long lives and clung greedily to them. What more did they get than those who died young? In the end, they all died too. Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus — they buried many others in their lifetimes, but eventually they were buried themselves. Any human life is short. And even that short time is filled with troubles, bad moods, and the burden of a failing body. So treat life as neither good nor bad in itself. Look backward and you see endless time stretching behind you. Look forward and you see endless time ahead. In that vastness, what difference is there between living three days or three lifetimes?

meditations_book-04.originalText:
Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most
compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both
words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect.
For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife,
dissembling, and ostentation.
meditations_book-04.plainEnglish: Always take the shortest path. The shortest path is the natural one. In everything you say and do, follow what is most sound and right. This approach will free you from all trouble, conflict, pretending, and showing off.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider
with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred
up. Am I then yet unwilling to go about that, for which I myself was
born and brought forth into this world? Or was I made for this, to
lay me down, and make much of myself in a warm bed? 'O but this is
pleasing.' And was it then for this that thou wert born, that thou
mightest enjoy pleasure? Was it not in very truth for this, that thou
mightest always be busy and in action? Seest thou not how all things
in the world besides, how every tree md plant, how sparrows and ants,
spiders and bees: how all in their kind are intent as it were orderly to
perform whatsoever (towards the preservation of this orderly universe)
naturally doth become and belong unto thin? And wilt not thou do that,
which belongs unto a man to do? Wilt not thou run to do that, which thy
nature doth require? 'But thou must have some rest.' Yes, thou must.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: In the morning when you don't want to get up, remind yourself right away: I am being stirred up to do a man's work. Am I really unwilling to do what I was born for? What I was brought into this world to do? Or was I made just to lie here and pamper myself in a warm bed? 'But this feels good.' Is that what you were born for — to enjoy pleasure? Weren't you born to always be busy and active? Look at everything else in the world. Every tree and plant, every sparrow and ant, spider and bee. They all focus on doing whatever naturally belongs to them for the good of the universe. Won't you do what belongs to a man? Won't you rush to do what your nature requires? 'But you need some rest.' Yes, you do.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Nature hath of that also, as well as of eating and drinking, allowed
thee a certain stint. But thou guest beyond thy stint, and beyond that
which would suffice, and in matter of action, there thou comest short of
that which thou mayest. It must needs be therefore, that thou dost not
love thyself, for if thou didst, thou wouldst also love thy nature, and
that which thy nature doth propose unto herself as her end. Others,
as many as take pleasure in their trade and profession, can even pine
themselves at their works, and neglect their bodies and their food for
it; and doest thou less honour thy nature, than an ordinary mechanic
his trade; or a good dancer his art? than a covetous man his silver, and
vainglorious man applause? These to whatsoever they take an affection,
can be content to want their meat and sleep, to further that every one
which he affects: and shall actions tending to the common good of
human society, seem more vile unto thee, or worthy of less respect and
intention?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Nature has given you limits for eating and drinking, just like everything else. But you go beyond what you need, beyond what would be enough. Yet when it comes to action, you fall short of what you could do. This means you don't love yourself. If you did, you would also love your nature and the purpose it sets for you. Look at others who love their work. They waste away at their tasks, skipping meals and rest. Do you honor your nature less than a craftsman honors his trade? Less than a dancer honors his art? Less than a greedy man honors his money, or a vain man honors praise? These people, when they care about something, will go without food and sleep to pursue it. So why do actions that serve the common good seem less worthy to you? Why do they deserve less effort and attention?

meditations_book-05.originalText:
How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent
adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and
tranquillity!
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: How easy it is to push away all those chaotic, outside thoughts and suddenly be at perfect rest and peace!

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is
according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that
may ensue upon it, ever deter thee. If it be right and honest to be
spoken or done, undervalue not thyself so much, as to be discouraged
from it. As for them, they have their own rational over-ruling part, and
their own proper inclination: which thou must not stand and look
about to take notice of, but go on straight, whither both thine own
particular, and the common nature do lead thee; and the way of both
these, is but one.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Know that you are fit and worthy to speak or do anything that follows nature. Don't let criticism or gossip stop you. If something is right and honest to say or do, don't think so little of yourself that you hold back. Other people have their own minds and their own ways. Don't waste time watching what they think. Keep moving straight ahead where your own nature and the common good lead you. The path of both is the same.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I
fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which
continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of
whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her
blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have
been provided, both of meat and drink. And lastly, which beareth me that
tread upon it, and beareth with me that so many ways do abuse it, or
so freely make use of it, so many ways to so many ends.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: I keep living according to nature until I fall and die, breathing my last breath into the same air I have always breathed. I will fall back to the same earth that gave my father his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk. This earth has fed me for so many years with food and drink. And this same earth carries me as I walk on it, and puts up with me even though I abuse it and use it freely in so many ways for so many purposes.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy
natural disability that way. Be it so: yet there be many other good
things, for the want of which thou canst not plead the want or natural
ability. Let them be seen in thee, which depend wholly from thee;
sincerity, gravity, laboriousness, contempt of pleasures; be not
querulous, be Content with little, be kind, be free; avoid all
superfluity, all vain prattling; be magnanimous. Doest not thou
perceive, how many things there be, which notwithstanding any pretence
of natural indisposition and unfitness, thou mightest have performed and
exhibited, and yet still thou doest voluntarily continue drooping
downwards? Or wilt thou say that it is through defect of thy natural
constitution, that thou art constrained to murmur, to be base and
wretched to flatter; now to accuse, and now to please, and pacify thy
body: to be vainglorious, to be so giddy-headed., and unsettled in thy
thoughts? nay (witnesses be the Gods) of all these thou mightest have
been rid long ago: only, this thou must have been contented with, to
have borne the blame of one that is somewhat slow and dull, wherein thou
must so exercise thyself, as one who neither doth much take to heart
this his natural defect, nor yet pleaseth himself in it.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: No one will admire you for clever, sharp speech — you simply don't have that gift. Fine. But there are many other good things you can't blame on lack of natural ability. Show the qualities that depend entirely on you: honesty, seriousness, hard work, rejection of pleasure. Don't complain. Be content with little. Be kind. Be free. Avoid excess and empty chatter. Be generous in spirit. Don't you see how many things you could have done and shown, despite any excuse about natural weakness? Yet you still choose to keep sinking down. Or will you claim that your nature forces you to complain, to be petty and miserable, to flatter others, to blame and please people, to pamper your body, to be vain and scattered in your thinking? No — the gods are my witnesses — you could have been free of all this long ago. You would only have to accept being called somewhat slow and dull. Work with that limitation without taking it too hard or taking pleasure in it.
