meditations_book-05.originalText: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation. Others there be, who though they stand not upon retaliation, to require any, yet they think with themselves nevertheless, that such a one is their debtor, and they know as their word is what they have done. Others again there be, who when they have done any such thing, do not so much as know what they have done; but are like unto the vine, which beareth her grapes, and when once she hath borne her own proper fruit, is contented and seeks for no further recompense. As a horse after a race, and a hunting dog when he hath hunted, and a bee when she hath made her honey, look not for applause and commendation; so neither doth that man that rightly doth understand his own nature when he hath done a good turn: but from one doth proceed to do another, even as the vine after she hath once borne fruit in her own proper season, is ready for another time. Thou therefore must be one of them, who what they do, barely do it without any further thought, and are in a manner insensible of what they do.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: There are different kinds of people when it comes to doing good. Some do a favor and immediately expect something back. They keep score. Others don't demand payback, but they still think the person owes them something. They remember what they did. Then there are those who do good and don't even think about it afterward. They're like a vine that bears grapes. Once it produces fruit, it's satisfied. It doesn't look for praise. A horse after running, a dog after hunting, a bee after making honey — none of them seek applause. The same goes for someone who truly understands their nature. After doing one good deed, they simply move on to the next. Like a vine that bears fruit in season and is ready to bear again. You should be like this. Do what you do without keeping track. Be almost unaware of your own good actions.

meditations_book-05.originalText: 'Nay but,' will some reply perchance, 'this very thing a rational man is bound unto, to understand what it is, that he doeth.' For it is the property, say they, of one that is naturally sociable, to be sensible, that he doth operate sociably: nay, and to desire, that the party him self that is sociably dealt with, should be sensible of it too. I answer, That which thou sayest is true indeed, but the true meaning of that which is said, thou dost not understand. And therefore art thou one of those first, whom I mentioned. For they also are led by a probable appearance of reason. But if thou dost desire to understand truly what it is that is said, fear not that thou shalt therefore give over any sociable action.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Someone might say, 'But a rational person should understand what they're doing.' They claim it's natural for social beings to know they're acting socially. They even want the other person to notice their good deed too. What you say is true, but you miss the real meaning. You're like those people I mentioned before. They follow what seems reasonable on the surface. But if you want to truly understand what this means, don't worry. You won't stop doing good things for others.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good
Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.'
Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not
every one for himself in particular alone.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: The Athenians used to pray like this: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or we should pray this way — openly and freely, not just for ourselves alone.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man,
riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it
is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this
man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing.
For as there, when we say of a physician, that he hath prescribed
anything, our meaning is, that he hath appointed this for that, as
subordinate and conducing to health: so here, whatsoever doth happen
unto any, is ordained unto him as a thing subordinate unto the fates,
and therefore do we say of such things, that they do συμβαίνειν, that
is, happen, or fall together; as of square stones, when either in
walls, or pyramids in a certain position they fit one another, and
agree as it were in an harmony, the masons say, that they do
συμβαίνειν; as if thou shouldest say, fall together: so that in the
general, though the things be divers that make it, yet the consent or
harmony itself is but one. And as the whole world is made up of all the
particular bodies of the world, one perfect and complete body, of the
same nature that particular bodies; so is the destiny of particular
causes and events one general one, of the same nature that particular
causes are. What I now say, even they that are mere idiots are not
ignorant of: for they say commonly τοῦτο ἔφερεν ἀυτῷ, that is, This
his destiny hath brought upon him. This therefore is by the fates
properly and particularly brought upon this, as that unto this in
particular is by the physician prescribed. These therefore let us
accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us
our physicians.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish:
We say the doctor prescribed riding for this patient, cold baths for another, and walking barefoot for a third. In the same way, the nature of the universe has prescribed sickness, blindness, or some loss for this person.

When we say a doctor prescribed something, we mean he chose it to help with health. So when anything happens to someone, it was chosen for them by fate. We say these things "happen together" — like square stones in walls or pyramids that fit perfectly. The builders say they "fall together" in harmony.

The whole world is made of individual bodies that form one complete body. In the same way, all particular events form one general destiny. Even simple people understand this. They say "this was brought to him by fate."

So what fate brings to each person is like what a doctor prescribes for each patient. We should accept both in the same way.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
For them also in themselves shall We find to contain
many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and
recovery, accept of them. Let the fulfilling and accomplishment of
those things which the common nature hath determined, be unto thee as
thy health. Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen,
though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing, as tending to that end, to the
health and welfare of the universe, and to Jove's happiness and
prosperity. For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced,
had it not conduced to the good of the universe. For neither doth any
ordinary particular nature bring anything to pass, that is not to
whatsoever is within the sphere of its own proper administration and
government agreeable and subordinate. For these two considerations then
thou must be well pleased with anything that doth happen unto thee.
First, because that for thee properly it was brought to pass, and unto
thee it was prescribed; and that from the very beginning by the series
and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto
thee. And secondly, because the good success and perfect welfare, and
indeed the very continuance of Him, that is the Administrator of the
whole, doth in a manner depend on it. For the whole (because whole,
therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt
cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of
parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it
is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some
sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with
anything that happeneth.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Medicine often tastes harsh, but we take it anyway because we hope it will heal us. Think of whatever the universe brings as your medicine. Accept what happens to you, even when it feels harsh and unpleasant. It all serves a purpose — the health of the whole universe and the will of God. Nothing would happen if it didn't serve the greater good. No force in nature creates anything that doesn't fit its proper role and purpose. So you should be content with whatever happens to you for two reasons. First, it was meant specifically for you. From the very beginning, through the chain of all causes, it was always heading your way. Second, the good of the whole universe — and its very survival — somehow depends on it. The universe is complete and perfect as it is. If you cut away any piece of it, you damage the whole thing. You break the connections that hold everything together. And that's exactly what you do when you complain about what happens to you. You're trying to cut away part of the whole.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Be not discontented, be not disheartened, be not out of hope, if
often it succeed not so well with thee punctually and precisely to do
all things according to the right dogmata, but being once cast off,
return unto them again: and as for those many and more frequent
occurrences, either of worldly distractions, or human infirmities, which
as a man thou canst not but in some measure be subject unto, be not thou
discontented with them; but however, love and affect that only which
thou dust return unto: a philosopher's life, and proper occupation after
the most exact manner. And when thou dust return to thy philosophy,
return not unto it as the manner of some is, after play and liberty as
it were, to their schoolmasters and pedagogues; but as they that have
sore eyes to their sponge and egg: or as another to his cataplasm; or
as others to their fomentations: so shalt not thou make it a matter of
ostentation at all to obey reason but of ease and comfort. And
remember that philosophy requireth nothing of thee, but what thy
nature requireth, and wouldest thou thyself desire anything that is
not according to nature? for which of these sayest thou; that which is
according to nature or against it, is of itself more kind and pleasing?
Is it not for that respect especially, that pleasure itself is to so
many men's hurt and overthrow, most prevalent, because esteemed commonly
most kind, and natural? But consider well whether magnanimity rather,
and true liberty, and true simplicity, and equanimity, and holiness;
whether these be not most kind and natural?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish:
Don't get discouraged, don't lose heart, don't give up hope if you often fail to live perfectly by the right principles. When you fall short, just return to them again. And don't be upset by all those frequent distractions from the world or human weaknesses that you can't help being subject to as a person. Instead, love and care only about what you return to: the philosopher's life and its proper work done with precision.

When you return to your philosophy, don't come back to it the way some people return to their teachers after playing around — as if it were a chore. Instead, come back like someone with sore eyes returns to a healing compress, or like a patient returns to a soothing treatment. Don't make obeying reason a show for others, but a source of relief and comfort.

Remember that philosophy asks nothing of you except what your nature already requires. Would you want anything that goes against nature? Which do you think is more kind and pleasing — what fits with nature or what fights against it? After all, isn't pleasure so harmful and destructive to many people precisely because they think it's the most natural thing?

But think about whether greatness of spirit, true freedom, true simplicity, calmness, and goodness — whether these aren't actually the most kind and natural.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
And prudency itself, what
more kind and amiable than it, when thou shalt truly consider with
thyself, what it is through all the proper objects of thy rational
intellectual faculty currently to go on without any fall or stumble?
As for the things of the world, their true nature is in a manner so
involved with obscurity, that unto many philosophers, and those no
mean ones, they seemed altogether incomprehensible, and the Stoics
themselves, though they judge them not altogether incomprehensible,
yet scarce and not without much difficulty, comprehensible, so that
all assent of ours is fallible, for who is he that is infallible in his
conclusions? From the nature of things, pass now unto their subjects
and matter: how temporary, how vile are they I such as may be in the
power and possession of some abominable loose liver, of some common
strumpet, of some notorious oppressor and extortioner. Pass from thence
to the dispositions of them that thou doest ordinarily converse with,
how hardly do we bear, even with the most loving and amiable! that I may
not say, how hard it is for us to bear even with our own selves, in such
obscurity, and impurity of things: in such and so continual a flux both
of the substances and time; both of the motions themselves, and things
moved; what it is that we can fasten upon; either to honour, and respect
especially; or seriously, and studiously to seek after; I cannot so much
as conceive For indeed they are things contrary.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: And wisdom itself — what could be kinder or more lovely than moving through life with your mind clear and steady, never stumbling? The truth is, the world around us is so clouded and unclear that many great philosophers found it completely impossible to understand. Even the Stoics, who think it can be grasped, say it's barely possible and only with great effort. So all our judgments might be wrong. Who among us never makes mistakes? Now think about the things themselves — how temporary and worthless they are. They might belong to some awful person, some prostitute, some cruel tyrant who bleeds people dry. Then look at the people you deal with every day. Even the most loving ones are hard to put up with — and let's be honest, it's hard to put up with ourselves too. Everything is so unclear and messy. Everything flows and changes constantly — the things themselves, time, motion, what moves. In all this chaos, what is there to really honor or chase after? I can't even imagine. These things pull us in opposite directions.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural
dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest
contented in those two things. First, that nothing shall happen unto
thee, which is not according to the nature of the universe. Secondly,
that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and
inward spirit. For it is not in any man's power to constrain thee to
transgress against him.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You must find comfort in knowing that your natural death will come, and not worry about the delay. Rest easy in two things. First, nothing will happen to you that goes against the nature of the universe. Second, you have the power to do nothing against your own god and inner spirit. No one can force you to betray what is sacred within you.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus
from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to
thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational
mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a
child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some
wild beast's soul?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: What am I doing with my soul right now? You must ask yourself this question often. What is my mind focused on at this moment? What kind of soul do I have right now? A child's? A young person's? A woman's? A tyrant's? Some animal's? Some wild beast's?

meditations_book-05.originalText: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is properly spoken of them. But as for those which by the vulgar are esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken for more.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You can see what things truly are by watching how people react to them. When someone hears real goods mentioned — wisdom, self-control, justice, courage — they feel satisfied. The word 'good' fits perfectly. They don't need to hear more. But when someone hears the things that most people call good, they always want to hear about more of them.

meditations_book-05.originalText: He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore, and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: People are fine hearing comedy that mocks virtue as long as it's just popular entertainment that everyone understands. Why is it that when comedians call virtues "good," no one gets offended and no excuse is needed? But when they praise wealth, pleasure, or status, we only accept it as harmless fun? Think about this more. Those same comedies mock the wealthy with jokes about how they own so much they don't even have a private place to relieve themselves. The audience laughs and applauds. So ask yourself: should we really respect and value these things that get mocked on stage? Are they truly the only good things in life?

meditations_book-05.originalText:
All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption
can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing
become a subsistent creature. Every part of mine then will by mutation
be disposed into a certain part of the whole world, and that in time
into another part; and so _in infinitum;_ by which kind of mutation, I
also became what I am, and so did they that begot me, and they before
them, and so upwards _in infinitum_. For so we may be allowed to speak,
though the age and government of the world, be to some certain periods
of time limited, and confined.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Everything I'm made of is either form or matter. Nothing can destroy either of these completely — I didn't come from nothing to begin with. Every part of me will change and become part of something else in the world. That part will then change into something else, and so on forever. This same process made me what I am. It made my parents what they were, and their parents before them, going back forever. We can think this way even though the world itself might have cycles and limits.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations. And as for their first inclination and motion, that they take from themselves. But their progress is right to the end and object, which is in their way, as it were, and lieth just before them: that is, which is feasible and possible, whether it be that which at the first they proposed to themselves, or no. For which reason also such actions are termed κατορθώσεις, to intimate the directness of the way, by which they are achieved.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Reason and rational thinking are satisfied with themselves and their own work. They start moving on their own. But they progress straight toward whatever goal lies in front of them — whatever is actually possible to achieve. It doesn't matter if this goal is the same one they started with or not. This is why such actions are called 'right achievements' — because they follow the most direct path.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Nothing must be thought to belong to a man, which doth not belong unto him as he is a man. These, the event of purposes, are not things required in a man. The nature of man doth not profess any such things. The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature. The end therefore of a man, or the _summum bonum_ whereby that end is fulfilled, cannot consist in the consummation of actions purposed and intended.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Don't think anything belongs to you that doesn't belong to you as a human being. The outcomes of your plans are not required of you as a person. Human nature doesn't promise such things. The final results of your actions have nothing to do with your nature as a human. So your purpose as a person — the highest good that fulfills that purpose — cannot depend on achieving the results you intended.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Again, concerning these outward worldly things, were it so that any of them did properly belong unto man, then would it not belong unto man, to condemn them and to stand in opposition with them. Neither would he be praiseworthy that can live without them; or he good, (if these were good indeed) who of his own accord doth deprive himself of any of them. But we see contrariwise, that the more a man doth withdraw himself from these wherein external pomp and greatness doth consist, or any other like these; or the better he doth bear with the loss of these, the better he is accounted.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think about external things again. If any of them truly belonged to human nature, then it wouldn't be right for a person to reject them or oppose them. A person who can live without them wouldn't deserve praise. And if these things were truly good, someone who gives them up willingly wouldn't be considered virtuous. But we see the opposite. The more someone withdraws from external honors and worldly greatness, or similar things, the better we think of them. The better someone handles losing these things, the more we respect them.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and happy.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Your mind becomes like your thoughts. The soul takes its color from whatever you imagine and think about. So dye it deeply with the right kind of thinking. For example: wherever you live, you can live well and be happy there. You might have to live at court — well, you can live well and be happy there too.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist. Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Everything is made for a purpose, and naturally moves toward that purpose. Where something finds its purpose, there it finds its good. Society is the proper good of rational beings. We have long known that we are made for society. Can anyone doubt that inferior things serve superior ones? The best things are made for each other. Things with souls are better than things without souls. And among things with souls, those with rational souls are best.

meditations_book-05.originalText: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things. Neither doth anything happen to any man, which in the ordinary course of nature as natural unto him doth not happen. Again, the same things happen unto others also.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Only a madman wants what can't be done. But it's impossible for bad people not to do bad things. Nothing happens to you that isn't part of the natural order of your life. Besides, the same things happen to everyone else too.

meditations_book-05.originalText: And truly, if either he that is ignorant that such a thing hath happened unto him, or he that is ambitious to be commended for his magnanimity, can be patient, and is not grieved: is it not a grievous thing, that either ignorance, or a vain desire to please and to be commended, should be more powerful and effectual than true prudence?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think about this: if someone who doesn't even know what happened to them can stay calm, or if someone who just wants praise for being tough can bear it without complaint — isn't it shameful that ignorance or vanity should be stronger than real wisdom?

meditations_book-05.originalText: As for the things themselves, they touch not the soul, neither can they have any access unto it: neither can they of themselves any ways either affect it, or move it. For she herself alone can affect and move herself, and according as the dogmata and opinions are, which she doth vouchsafe herself; so are those things which, as accessories, have any co-existence with her.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Things themselves cannot touch your soul. They have no way to reach it or affect it. Only the soul can affect and move itself. The things that seem connected to your soul are shaped by the beliefs and opinions you choose to accept.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound
to do them good, and to bear with them. But as he may oppose any of our
true proper actions, so man is unto me but as a thing indifferent: even
as the sun, or the wind, or some wild beast. By some of these it may be,
that some operation or other of mine, may be hindered; however, of my
mind and resolution itself, there can be no let or impediment, by reason
of that ordinary constant both exception (or reservation wherewith it
inclineth) and ready conversion of objects; from that which may not be,
to that which may be, which in the prosecution of its inclinations, as
occasion serves, it doth observe. For by these the mind doth turn and
convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose. So that
what before was the impediment, is now the principal object of her
working; and that which before was in her way, is now her readiest way.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Look at it this way: other people are closest to us. We should help them and put up with them. But when someone blocks our right actions, that person becomes just another neutral thing to me — like the sun, wind, or a wild animal. Some of these might slow down what I'm doing. But nothing can block my mind and will. My mind has a built-in ability to shift focus and adapt. It turns away from what can't be done toward what can be done. The mind converts any obstacle into its new target. What was blocking the path becomes the work itself. What was in the way becomes the way forward.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and
that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So
also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and
is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the
very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use,
and by whom also thy life is governed.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Honor what is highest and most powerful in the world — the force that uses all things and governs all things. Do the same in yourself. Honor what is highest and most powerful in you, which is the same kind of thing. It is the very same force that lives in you, that turns everything else to its own use, and that governs your life.

meditations_book-05.originalText: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong. If the whole city be not hurt by this, neither am I certainly. And if the whole be not, why should I make it my private grievance? consider rather what it is wherein he is overseen that is thought to have done the wrong.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: What doesn't hurt the city itself cannot hurt any citizen. Remember this rule whenever you feel wronged. If the whole city isn't harmed by this, then neither am I. And if the whole isn't harmed, why should I take it personally? Think instead about where the person who seems to have wronged you has gone astray.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Again, often meditate how swiftly all things that subsist, and all things that are done in the world, are carried away, and as it were conveyed out of sight: for both the substance themselves, we see as a flood, are in a continual flux; and all actions in a perpetual change; and the causes themselves, subject to a thousand alterations, neither is there anything almost, that may ever be said to be now settled and constant.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think often about how quickly everything that exists, and everything that happens in the world, gets swept away and disappears from sight. The things themselves flow like a river in constant motion. All actions are always changing. Even the causes behind things shift in a thousand ways. There is almost nothing you can say is fixed and permanent.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Next unto this, and which follows upon it, consider both the infiniteness of the time already past, and the immense vastness of that which is to come, wherein all things are to be resolved and annihilated. Art not thou then a very fool, who for these things, art either puffed up with pride, or distracted with cares, or canst find in thy heart to make such moans as for a thing that would trouble thee for a very long time? Consider the whole universe whereof thou art but a very little part, and the whole age of the world together, whereof but a short and very momentary portion is allotted unto thee, and all the fates and destinies together, of which how much is it that comes to thy part and share!
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Think about this next: the endless time that came before you, and the vast time that will come after, when everything dissolves into nothing. Aren't you being foolish when you get puffed up with pride or worry yourself sick over things? Or when you complain as if something would bother you forever? Think about the whole universe — you are just a tiny part of it. Think about all of time — you get only a brief moment. Think about everything that happens in the world — how little of it actually touches your life.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Again: another doth trespass against me. Let him look to that. He is master of his own disposition, and of his own operation. I for my part am in the meantime in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess: and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Someone wrongs me again. That's his problem. He controls his own thoughts and actions. Meanwhile, I have what universal nature intended for me to have. And I do what my own nature tells me to do.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to
any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither
suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself,
and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members.
But if at any time they do reflect and rebound upon the mind and
understanding (as in an united and compacted body it must needs;) then
must thou not go about to resist sense and feeling, it being natural.
However let not thy understanding to this natural sense and feeling,
which whether unto our flesh pleasant or painful, is unto us nothing
properly, add an opinion of either good or bad and all is well.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Don't let the ruling part of your mind be controlled by any physical pain or pleasure. Keep it separate from these feelings. Let those sensations stay in the parts of your body where they belong. But if they do bounce back and affect your mind (which they will, since body and mind are connected), don't try to resist the feeling itself. That's natural. Just don't let your mind add the judgment that the sensation is either good or bad. What happens to our flesh, pleasant or painful, means nothing to us really. If you avoid that judgment, all is well.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times
affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well
pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and
performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of
himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: To live with the Gods. Someone lives with the Gods when they show them a soul that is content and pleased with whatever happens to them. They do whatever pleases that spirit — part of themselves — that Zeus has given to each person as their guide and ruler.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose
arm holes, are offensive. What can he do? such is his breath naturally,
and such are his arm holes; and from such, such an effect, and such
a smell must of necessity proceed. 'O, but the man (sayest thou) hath
understanding in him, and might of himself know, that he by standing
near, cannot choose but offend.' And thou also (God bless thee!) hast
understanding. Let thy reasonable faculty, work upon his reasonable
faculty; show him his fault, admonish him. If he hearken unto thee, thou
hast cured him, and there will be no more occasion of anger.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Don't get angry with someone whose breath stinks or whose armpits smell bad. What can he do? That's just how his breath is naturally, and that's how his armpits are. From such things, such smells must follow. 'But,' you say, 'the man has a mind and should know that standing close will offend people.' Well, you have a mind too. Use your reason to work on his reason. Show him the problem. Tell him about it. If he listens, you've helped him, and there's no need to be angry anymore.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As
thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such
place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if
they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than
thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged.
Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a
great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will
continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and
my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable
creature, regulated and directed.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You might think, 'I'll go somewhere with no troublemakers or immoral people.' But why? You can live the same way right here. If you plan to be virtuous when you escape to some perfect place, you can be virtuous now. And if people won't let you live as you should, you can leave life itself rather than abandon your principles. But don't think of yourself as wronged. Just say, 'There's smoke here; I'll step outside.' What's the big deal? Until something forces me out, I'll stay free. No one will stop me from doing what I choose. And what I choose will always be guided by my nature as a rational, social being.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for
community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that
are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those
which are best, as it were in an harmony. Seest thou not how it hath
sub-ordinated, and co-ordinated? and how it hath distributed unto
everything according to its worth? and those which have the pre-eminency
and superiority above all, hath it united together, into a mutual
consent and agreement.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: The rational force that governs the universe is meant for community and cooperation. It has made the worse things serve the best ones. It has joined the best things together in harmony. Don't you see how it has organized everything? It has given each thing what it deserves. And those things that are highest and best, it has united them so they work together in agreement.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards
thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy
children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy
domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast
neither by word or deed wronged any of them? Remember withal through how
many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able
to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is
accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee
been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over
with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised?
towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself
kindly, and discreetly?
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: How have you treated the gods? Your parents? Your brothers and sisters? Your wife? Your children? Your teachers? Those who raised you? Your friends? Your household? Your servants? Can you say that you have never wronged any of them in word or deed? Remember all the things you have been through. Remember how much you have endured. The story of your life is already full. Your work is done. How many good things have you recognized? How many pleasures and pains have you faced with indifference? How many impressive things have you dismissed as worthless? How many difficult, unreasonable people have you treated with kindness and wisdom?

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is
both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that
understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of
that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and
through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it
were this universe by certain periods of time.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Why should foolish, ignorant souls disturb what is wise and thoughtful? And what is this wise thing? It is the soul that understands the beginning and the end. It truly knows the rational essence that flows through all existing things and through all time, always staying the same. It arranges and manages the universe in regular cycles.

meditations_book-05.originalText: Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name. And what is that but an empty sound, and a rebounding echo? Those things which in this life are dearest unto us, and of most account, they are in themselves but vain, putrid, contemptible. The most weighty and serious, if rightly esteemed, but as puppies, biting one another: or untoward children, now laughing and then crying. As for faith, and modesty, and justice, and truth, they long since, as one of the poets hath it, have abandoned this spacious earth, and retired themselves unto heaven.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: Very soon you will be nothing but ashes or bones. Maybe a name will remain, maybe not even that. And what is a name anyway? Just empty sound and an echo. The things we treasure most in life are really worthless, rotten, and pitiful. The most serious and important matters, if you see them clearly, are like puppies snapping at each other. Or like children who laugh one moment and cry the next. As for faith, decency, justice, and truth — as the poet said, they left this wide earth long ago and went back to heaven.

meditations_book-05.originalText: What is it then that doth keep thee here, if things sensible be so mutable and unsettled? and the senses so obscure, and so fallible? and our souls nothing but an exhalation of blood? and to be in credit among such, be but vanity? What is it that thou dost stay for? an extinction, or a translation; either of them with a propitious and contented mind. But still that time come, what will content thee? what else, but to worship and praise the Gods; and to do good unto men. To bear with them, and to forbear to do them any wrong. And for all external things belonging either to this thy wretched body, or life, to remember that they are neither thine, nor in thy power.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: What keeps you here then, if physical things are always changing and unstable? If your senses are unclear and unreliable? If your soul is nothing more than vapors from blood? If being respected by people like this means nothing? What are you waiting for? Death, or some transformation — either one with a calm and willing mind. But until that time comes, what will satisfy you? Only this: honor the gods, do good for other people. Put up with them, and don't harm them. And remember that all external things — whether they belong to this failing body or to life itself — are not really yours and not under your control.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the
right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou
wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as
of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their
own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that
their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of
righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: You can always make progress if you choose the right path. In both your thoughts and actions, follow a true method. Two things are shared by all souls — God's, humans', and every rational being's. First, nothing can stop them from doing their proper work. Second, their happiness comes from wanting what is right and doing what is right. This is where their desires should end.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending
from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what
doth it concern me? And wherein can the public be hurt? For thou must
not altogether be carried by conceit and common opinion: as for help
thou must afford that unto them after thy best ability, and as occasion
shall require, though they sustain damage, but in these middle or
worldly things; but however do not thou conceive that they are truly
hurt thereby: for that is not right. But as that old foster-father
in the comedy, being now to take his leave doth with a great deal of
ceremony, require his foster-child's rhombus, or rattle-top, remembering
nevertheless that it is but a rhombus; so here also do thou likewise.
For indeed what is all this pleading and public bawling for at the
courts? O man, hast thou forgotten what those things are! yea but they
are things that others much care for, and highly esteem of. Wilt thou
therefore be a fool too? Once I was; let that suffice.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish: If this is not my fault, and doesn't come from any wrong I've done, and it doesn't hurt the common good — why should I worry? How could it really hurt anyone? Don't let yourself get swept up by what people think. Help others when you can, as best you can, when the moment calls for it. They might lose some worldly things, but don't think they're truly harmed by that. That's not the right way to see it. It's like that old guardian in the play who makes a big show of asking for his child's toy rattle back when he's leaving — but he knows it's just a rattle. Do the same here. What is all this arguing and shouting in the courts really about? Have you forgotten what these things actually are? Yes, but other people care deeply about them and think they matter. Will you be a fool too? I was once. Let that be enough.

meditations_book-05.originalText:
Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be
εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless.

For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy
lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the
soul, good desires, good actions.
meditations_book-05.plainEnglish:
Let death come when it wants and where it wants. I can still be a happy man.

A happy man is someone who gives himself a good life while he's alive. A good life means having good thoughts, good desires, and doing good things.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
The matter itself, of which the universe doth consist, is of itself
very tractable and pliable. That rational essence that doth govern it,
hath in itself no cause to do evil. It hath no evil in itself; neither
can it do anything that is evil: neither can anything be hurt by it. And
all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: The basic stuff that makes up the universe is flexible and easy to work with. The rational force that governs it has no reason to do evil. It contains no evil in itself. It cannot do anything evil, and nothing can be harmed by it. Everything happens according to its will and plan.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether
only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or
commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for
that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties
and actions of our lives.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Let it be the same to you whether you are half frozen or warm. Whether you have barely slept or slept well. Whether people criticize you or praise you as you do your duty. Whether you are dying or doing something else — dying is also one of the duties and actions of life.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of
anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Look inside yourself. Don't let the real nature or true value of anything slip past you before you fully understand it.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
All substances come soon to their change, and either they shall
be resolved by way of exhalation (if so be that all things shall be
reunited into one substance), or as others maintain, they shall be
scattered and dispersed. As for that Rational Essence by which all
things are governed, as it best understandeth itself, both its own
disposition, and what it doth, and what matter it hath to do with and
accordingly doth all things; so we that do not, no wonder, if we wonder
at many things, the reasons whereof we cannot comprehend.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: All things change quickly. They either dissolve back into one substance, or they scatter and break apart—depending on which theory you believe. The rational force that governs everything understands itself perfectly. It knows its own nature, what it does, and what it works with. So it acts accordingly. We don't understand these things, so no wonder we're amazed by so much that we can't grasp.

meditations_book-06.originalText: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: The best kind of revenge is not to become like them.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable
kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in
thy mind.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Let this be your only joy and comfort: to move from one kind act to another without stopping, always keeping God in your mind.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn
itself; so it maketh both itself to be, and everything that happeneth,
to appear unto itself, as it will itself.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: The rational mind has complete power over itself. It can stir itself up or calm itself down. It makes itself into whatever it chooses to be. And it decides how everything that happens will appear to it.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
According to the nature of the universe all things particular are
determined, not according to any other nature, either about compassing
and containing; or within, dispersed and contained; or without,
depending. Either this universe is a mere confused mass, and an
intricate context of things, which shall in time be scattered and
dispersed again: or it is an union consisting of order, and administered
by Providence. If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer
in this fortuit confusion and commixtion? or why should I take care for
anything else, but that as soon as may be I may be earth again? And
why should I trouble myself any more whilst I seek to please the Gods?
Whatsoever I do, dispersion is my end, and will come upon me whether I
will or no. But if the latter be, then am not I religious in vain;
then will I be quiet and patient, and put my trust in Him, who is the
Governor of all.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Everything in the universe follows one law, not many different ones. Either the universe is just a jumbled mess that will fall apart someday, or it's an ordered whole guided by Providence. If it's just chaos, why would I want to stay here longer in this random confusion? Why care about anything except returning to dust as quickly as possible? Why bother trying to please the gods? Whatever I do, I'll fall apart in the end anyway. But if the universe has order and purpose, then my faith isn't wasted. Then I can be calm and patient, and trust the one who governs everything.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to
be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may
be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs. For so shalt
thou be the better able to keep thy part another time, and to maintain
the harmony, if thou dost use thyself to this continually; once out,
presently to have recourse unto it, and to begin again.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: When hard times force you into some kind of distress, get back to yourself as quickly as you can. Don't stay out of tune longer than you have to. This way you'll be better able to play your part next time and keep the harmony. Make this a habit — whenever you're thrown off, immediately return to your center and start again.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and
a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also;
nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse
be continually. So let the court and thy philosophy be unto thee. Have
recourse unto it often, and comfort thyself in her, by whom it is that
those other things are made tolerable unto thee, and thou also in those
things not intolerable unto others.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: If you had both a stepmother and a natural mother alive at the same time, you would honor and respect the stepmother too. But you would always turn to your natural mother for comfort and help. Let the court and your philosophy be like this for you. Turn to philosophy often and find comfort in it. Philosophy makes those other courtly things bearable for you, and helps you be bearable to others in return.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
How marvellous useful it is for a man to represent unto himself
meats, and all such things that are for the mouth, under a right
apprehension and imagination! as for example: This is the carcass of a
fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog. And again more generally; This
phalernum, this excellent highly commended wine, is but the bare juice
of an ordinary grape. This purple robe, but sheep's hairs, dyed with
the blood of a shellfish. So for coitus, it is but the attrition of an
ordinary base entrail, and the excretion of a little vile snivel, with
a certain kind of convulsion: according to Hippocrates his opinion. How
excellent useful are these lively fancies and representations of things,
thus penetrating and passing through the objects, to make their true
nature known and apparent! This must thou use all thy life long, and
upon all occasions: and then especially, when matters are apprehended
as of great worth and respect, thy art and care must be to uncover
them, and to behold their vileness, and to take away from them all those
serious circumstances and expressions, under which they made so grave
a show. For outward pomp and appearance is a great juggler; and then
especially art thou most in danger to be beguiled by it, when (to
a man's thinking) thou most seemest to be employed about matters of
moment.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: How wonderfully useful it is to see food and other pleasures as they really are! For example: This is a dead fish. This is a dead bird. This is a dead pig. And more generally: This expensive wine that everyone praises is just squeezed grape juice. This purple robe is just sheep hair dyed with shellfish blood. Sex is just rubbing body parts together and releasing fluids with some spasms — that's what Hippocrates said. How useful these clear pictures are! They cut right through appearances to show what things really are. You must do this your whole life, especially when something seems very important or impressive. Your job is to strip away the fancy packaging and see how ordinary it really is underneath. Outward show is a master of deception. You are most likely to be fooled by it when you think you're dealing with something that really matters.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
See what Crates pronounceth concerning Xenocrates himself.

Those things which the common sort of people do admire, are most
of them such things as are very general, and may be comprehended under
things merely natural, or naturally affected and qualified: as stones,
wood, figs, vines, olives. Those that be admired by them that are more
moderate and restrained, are comprehended under things animated: as
flocks and herds. Those that are yet more gentle and curious, their
admiration is commonly confined to reasonable creatures only; not in
general as they are reasonable, but as they are capable of art, or of
some craft and subtile invention: or perchance barely to reasonable
creatures; as they that delight in the possession of many slaves. But
he that honours a reasonable soul in general, as it is reasonable and
naturally sociable, doth little regard anything else: and above all
things is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and
exercise both of reason and sociableness: and thereby doth co-operate
with him, of whose nature he doth also participate; God.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish:
See what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.

Most people admire very basic things. These are natural objects like stones, wood, figs, vines, and olives. People who are more thoughtful admire living things like flocks and herds. Those who are even more refined focus on reasoning creatures. But not because they can reason — because they can do skilled work or clever inventions. Or maybe they just like owning many slaves. But someone who honors the reasoning soul itself — because it can think and naturally connects with others — cares little for anything else. Above all, he works to keep his own soul in the constant practice of reason and fellowship. In this way he works together with the one whose nature he shares: God.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Some things hasten to be, and others to be no more. And even
whatsoever now is, some part thereof hath already perished. Perpetual
fluxes and alterations renew the world, as the perpetual course of time
doth make the age of the world (of itself infinite) to appear always
fresh and new. In such a flux and course of all things, what of these
things that hasten so fast away should any man regard, since among all
there is not any that a man may fasten and fix upon? as if a man would
settle his affection upon some ordinary sparrow living by him, who is no
sooner seen, than out of sight. For we must not think otherwise of our
lives, than as a mere exhalation of blood, or of an ordinary respiration
of air. For what in our common apprehension is, to breathe in the air
and to breathe it out again, which we do daily: so much is it and no
more, at once to breathe out all thy respirative faculty into that
common air from whence but lately (as being but from yesterday, and
to-day), thou didst first breathe it in, and with it, life.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Some things rush to exist, and others rush to disappear. Even what exists now is already partly gone. Everything flows and changes constantly. This renews the world, just like time itself makes the infinite world always seem fresh and new. In this constant flow of everything, why should anyone care about these things that pass so quickly? There's nothing you can hold onto. It would be like falling in love with a sparrow that flies by — you see it, then it's gone. Think of your life the same way. It's just like breathing out steam, or taking a breath of air. Every day you breathe in and breathe out. That's all there is to it. One day you'll breathe out your last breath into the same air you've been breathing since yesterday and today — the air that gave you life.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Not vegetative spiration, it is not surely (which plants have) that in this life should be so dear unto us; nor sensitive respiration, the proper life of beasts, both tame and wild; nor this our imaginative faculty; nor that we are subject to be led and carried up and down by the strength of our sensual appetites; or that we can gather, and live together; or that we can feed: for that in effect is no better, than that we can void the excrements of our food. What is it then that should be dear unto us? to hear a clattering noise? if not that, then neither to be applauded by the tongues of men. For the praises of many tongues, is in effect no better than the clattering of so many tongues. If then neither applause, what is there remaining that should be dear unto thee? This I think: that in all thy motions and actions thou be moved, and restrained according to thine own true natural constitution and Construction only.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish:
The basic functions of life shouldn't be what we value most. Not breathing like plants do. Not the animal instincts we share with wild and tame beasts. Not our ability to imagine things. Not being pushed around by our physical desires. Not gathering together or eating — that's no better than being able to excrete waste.

So what should matter to us? Hearing applause? No — and if not that, then not the praise of many voices either. The cheers of a crowd are really just noise.

If applause means nothing, what's left that should be precious to you? This: that in everything you do, you move and hold back according to your own true nature alone.

meditations_book-06.originalText: And to this even ordinary arts and professions do lead us. For it is that which every art doth aim at, that whatsoever it is, that is by art effected and prepared, may be fit for that work that it is prepared for. This is the end that he that dresseth the vine, and he that takes upon him either to tame colts, or to train up dogs, doth aim at. What else doth the education of children, and all learned professions tend unto? Certainly then it is that, which should be dear unto us also. If in this particular it go well with thee, care not for the obtaining of other things. But is it so, that thou canst not but respect other things also? Then canst not thou truly be free? then canst thou not have self-content: then wilt thou ever be subject to passions. For it is not possible, but that thou must be envious, and jealous, and suspicious of them whom thou knowest can bereave thee of such things; and again, a secret underminer of them, whom thou seest in present possession of that which is dear unto thee. To be short, he must of necessity be full of confusion within himself, and often accuse the Gods, whosoever stands in need of these things. But if thou shalt honour and respect thy mind only, that will make thee acceptable towards thyself, towards thy friends very tractable; and conformable and concordant with the Gods; that is, accepting with praises whatsoever they shall think good to appoint and allot unto thee.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Even ordinary crafts and jobs teach us this lesson. Every art aims for the same thing: whatever it creates should be fit for its purpose. This is what the vine-dresser wants, and the person who trains horses or dogs. What else does the education of children and all learning aim for? This should matter to us too. If you do well in this one thing, don't worry about getting other things. But can't you help wanting other things too? Then you can't truly be free. You can't be content with yourself. You will always be ruled by your emotions. You will be envious and jealous and suspicious of people who can take these things from you. You will secretly work against people who have what you want. In short, anyone who needs these things must be confused inside and often blame the gods. But if you honor and respect only your mind, that will make you happy with yourself, easy to get along with, and in harmony with the gods. You will accept with gratitude whatever they decide to give you.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Under, above, and about, are the motions of the elements; but
the motion of virtue, is none of those motions, but is somewhat more
excellent and divine. Whose way (to speed and prosper in it) must be
through a way, that is not easily comprehended.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Around us, above us, and below us, the elements are always moving. But virtue moves differently. Its motion is something higher and more divine. To make progress in virtue, you must travel a path that is not easy to understand.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of
them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they
themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they
have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if
a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived
before him.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Who wouldn't be amazed by people like this? They won't speak well of those around them right now - the people they actually live and work with. Yet they desperately want future generations to praise them - people they will never meet or even see. It's like being upset that people who lived before you didn't praise you.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee
cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in
general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that
very possible unto thee also.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Don't think anything is impossible for you if other people can do it. If you see that something is possible for any person, then it's possible for you too — even if it takes effort.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Suppose that at the palestra somebody hath all to-torn thee with
his nails, and hath broken thy head. Well, thou art wounded. Yet thou
dost not exclaim; thou art not offended with him. Thou dost not suspect
him for it afterwards, as one that watcheth to do thee a mischief. Yea
even then, though thou dost thy best to save thyself from him, yet not
from him as an enemy. It is not by way of any suspicious indignation,
but by way of gentle and friendly declination. Keep the same mind and
disposition in other parts of thy life also. For many things there be,
which we must conceit and apprehend, as though we had had to do with an
antagonist at the palestra. For as I said, it is very possible for us to
avoid and decline, though we neither suspect, nor hate.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Imagine someone at the wrestling ground scratches you badly with their nails and cuts your head. You're hurt, but you don't cry out. You're not angry with them. You don't suspect them of trying to harm you on purpose. Even when you try to protect yourself from them, you don't treat them as an enemy. You avoid them not out of angry suspicion, but with calm and friendly caution. Keep this same attitude in the rest of your life too. There are many situations we should handle as if we're dealing with a wrestling partner. As I said, we can avoid and protect ourselves without suspicion or hatred.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me,
that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most
gladly retract. For it is the truth that I seek after, by which I am
sure that never any man was hurt; and as sure, that he is hurt that
continueth in any error, or ignorance whatsoever.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: If anyone corrects me and shows me clearly that I'm wrong in my thinking or actions, I'll gladly change my mind. I'm after the truth, and I know that truth never hurt anyone. But I also know that staying wrong or ignorant always hurts you.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
I for my part will do what belongs unto me; as for other things,
whether things unsensible or things irrational; or if rational, yet
deceived and ignorant of the true way, they shall not trouble or
distract me. For as for those creatures which are not endued with reason
and all other things and-matters of the world whatsoever I freely, and
generously, as one endued with reason, of things that have none, make
use of them. And as for men, towards them as naturally partakers of the
same reason, my care is to carry myself sociably. But whatsoever it is
that thou art about, remember to call upon the Gods. And as for the time
how long thou shalt live to do these things, let it be altogether
indifferent unto thee, for even three such hours are sufficient.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: I will do what is mine to do. Other things won't trouble me — whether they are objects without feeling, or animals acting on instinct, or even people who have reason but are confused and don't know the right path. I use things without reason freely and generously, as someone with reason should. With other people, since they share the same rational nature, I try to be social and cooperative. Whatever you are doing, remember to call on the gods. As for how long you will live to do these things, don't worry about it. Even three hours would be enough.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once
dead both came to one. For either they were both resumed into those
original rational essences from whence all things in the world are
propagated; or both after one fashion were scattered into atoms.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Alexander the Great and the man who took care of his mules both ended up the same way when they died. Either they both returned to the universal reason from which all things come, or they both scattered into atoms the same way.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Consider how many different things, whether they concern our
bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of
us, and so thou wilt not wonder if many more things or rather all things
that are done, can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and
general, which we call the world.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Think about how many different things happen in our bodies and minds at the same moment. Then you won't be surprised that many more things — or really all things — can exist at the same time in what we call the world.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus
is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and
utter out in order every letter of it? And if any shall begin to gainsay
thee, and quarrel with thee about it; wilt thou quarrel with him again,
or rather go on meekly as thou hast begun, until thou hast numbered out
every letter? Here then likewise remember, that every duty that belongs
unto a man doth consist of some certain letters or numbers as it were,
to which without any noise or tumult keeping thyself thou must orderly
proceed to thy proposed end, forbearing to quarrel with him that would
quarrel and fall out with thee.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: If someone asked you how to spell the name Antoninus, you would focus and say each letter in order. And if someone argued with you about it, you wouldn't argue back. You would just keep going calmly until you finished spelling out every letter. Remember this when doing your duties. Each task has its steps, like letters in a word. Stay quiet and orderly. Move toward your goal without fighting back when others want to quarrel with you.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Is it not a cruel thing to forbid men to affect those things, which
they conceive to agree best with their own natures, and to tend most
to their own proper good and behoof? But thou after a sort deniest them
this liberty, as often as thou art angry with them for their sins. For
surely they are led unto those sins whatsoever they be, as to
their proper good and commodity. But it is not so (thou wilt object
perchance). Thou therefore teach them better, and make it appear unto
them: but be not thou angry with them.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Isn't it cruel to stop people from pursuing what they think is best for them? What they believe will help them most? But you deny them this freedom every time you get angry at their mistakes. They are drawn to these wrong choices because they think it will benefit them. You might say that's not true. Then teach them better. Show them the truth. But don't be angry with them.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the
tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of
the body.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Death is an end to what your senses tell you, the control of your emotions, the mistakes of your mind, and being trapped in your body.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a
shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest
of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new
tincture from the court. For it may happen if thou dost not take heed.
Keep thyself therefore, truly simple, good, sincere, grave, free
from all ostentation, a lover of that which is just, religious, kind,
tender-hearted, strong and vigorous to undergo anything that becomes
thee. Endeavour to continue such, as philosophy (hadst thou wholly and
constantly applied thyself unto it) would have made, and secured thee.
Worship the Gods, procure the welfare of men, this life is short.
Charitable actions, and a holy disposition, is the only fruit of this
earthly life.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish:
If your body can handle this kind of life, it's shameful for your soul to give up first. Be careful not to let the court corrupt you. You might become just another Caesar instead of a philosopher if you're not careful.

Stay truly simple, good, honest, serious, and without show. Love justice. Be religious, kind, tender-hearted, and strong enough to do what you must. Try to remain the person philosophy would have made you if you had stuck with it completely.

Worship the gods. Help other people. This life is short. Kind actions and a holy heart are the only things that matter in this earthly life.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Do all things as becometh the disciple of Antoninus Pius. Remember his resolute constancy in things that were done by him according to reason, his equability in all things, his sanctity; the cheerfulness of his countenance, his sweetness, and how free he was from all vainglory; how careful to come to the true and exact knowledge of matters in hand, and how he would by no means give over till he did fully, and plainly understand the whole state of the business; and how patiently, and without any contestation he would bear with them, that did unjustly condemn him: how he would never be over-hasty in anything, nor give ear to slanders and false accusations, but examine and observe with best diligence the several actions and dispositions of men.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Do everything as a student of Antoninus Pius would. Remember how steady he was when he acted on reason. Remember his calmness in all things, his goodness, the cheerfulness in his face, his kindness. Remember how he never sought praise for himself. Remember how carefully he worked to truly understand whatever he was dealing with. He would never give up until he fully grasped the whole situation. Remember how patiently he dealt with people who wrongly criticized him, never arguing back. He was never rushed in anything. He didn't listen to gossip or false charges. Instead, he carefully watched and studied how people actually behaved.

meditations_book-06.originalText: Again, how he was no backbiter, nor easily frightened, nor suspicious, and in his language free from all affectation and curiosity: and how easily he would content himself with few things, as lodging, bedding, clothing, and ordinary nourishment, and attendance. How able to endure labour, how patient; able through his spare diet to continue from morning to evening without any necessity of withdrawing before his accustomed hours to the necessities of nature: his uniformity and constancy in matter of friendship. How he would bear with them that with all boldness and liberty opposed his opinions; and even rejoice if any man could better advise him: and lastly, how religious he was without superstition. All these things of him remember, that whensoever thy last hour shall come upon thee, it may find thee, as it did him, ready for it in the possession of a good conscience.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: He never talked behind people's backs. He wasn't easily scared or suspicious. His speech was natural and straightforward. He was happy with simple things - basic housing, plain bedding, simple clothes, ordinary food, and minimal help. He could work hard for hours. He was patient. His light eating let him go from morning to evening without needing breaks before his usual times. He was steady and loyal in friendship. He welcomed people who boldly disagreed with him. He was even glad when someone gave him better advice. He was deeply religious but not superstitious. Remember all this about him. When your last hour comes, may it find you as ready as he was, with a clear conscience.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Stir up thy mind, and recall thy wits again from thy natural
dreams, and visions, and when thou art perfectly awoken, and canst
perceive that they were but dreams that troubled thee, as one newly
awakened out of another kind of sleep look upon these worldly things
with the same mind as thou didst upon those, that thou sawest in thy
sleep.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: Wake up your mind. Pull your thoughts back from daydreams and fantasies. When you are fully awake and can see that they were just dreams that bothered you, look at the things of this world the same way. Treat them like you would treat what you saw while sleeping.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
I consist of body and soul. Unto my body all things are
indifferent, for of itself it cannot affect one thing more than another
with apprehension of any difference; as for my mind, all things which
are not within the verge of her own operation, are indifferent unto her,
and for her own operations, those altogether depend of her; neither
does she busy herself about any, but those that are present; for as
for future and past operations, those also are now at this present
indifferent unto her.
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: I am made of body and soul. To my body, all things are the same. My body cannot tell the difference between one thing and another. As for my mind, everything outside its control means nothing to it. The mind only cares about its own actions. And those actions depend completely on the mind itself. The mind only deals with what is happening right now. Past and future actions don't matter to it in this moment.

meditations_book-06.originalText:
As long as the foot doth that which belongeth unto it to do, and
the hand that which belongs unto it, their labour, whatsoever it be, is
not unnatural. So a man as long as he doth that which is proper unto
a man, his labour cannot be against nature; and if it be not against
nature, then neither is it hurtful unto him. But if it were so that
happiness did consist in pleasure: how came notorious robbers, impure
abominable livers, parricides, and tyrants, in so large a measure to
have their part of pleasures?
meditations_book-06.plainEnglish: As long as the foot does what a foot is meant to do, and the hand does what a hand is meant to do, their work is natural. The same is true for a person. As long as he does what a person is meant to do, his work cannot go against nature. And if it doesn't go against nature, then it cannot harm him. But if happiness really came from pleasure, then why do thieves, corrupt people, murderers, and tyrants get so much pleasure?

meditations_book-06.originalText:
Dost thou not see, how even those that profess mechanic arts,
though in some respect they be no better than mere idiots, yet they
stick close to the course of their trade, neither can they find in
their heart to decline from it: and is it not a grievous thing that
an architect, or a physician shall respect the course and mysteries of
